questions.stem: Which technique most reliably improves a complex prompt containing instructions, reference material and examples?

options.text: Writing it in a single long paragraph so nothing is missed.
Delimiting the parts with clear structure — XML tags or headed sections — so instructions cannot be confused with data.
Using capital letters for emphasis throughout.
Repeating the instruction five times.

questions.explanation: Explicit structure separates the roles of each block: this is the instruction, this is the document, these are the examples. It is the single highest-leverage change for long prompts, and it also makes injection through the data block far less confusing to the model.

snippet.title: Structured prompt
snippet.code:
<instructions>
Classify the ticket into exactly one category from <categories>.
Return only the JSON object described in <output_format>.
</instructions>

<categories>billing, outage, feature_request, how_to</categories>

<ticket>
{{ticket_text}}
</ticket>

<output_format>{"category": "...", "confidence": 0.0}</output_format>

questions.stem: A classification prompt produces inconsistent output formats. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add two or three examples showing input and the exact expected output.
Ask the model to try harder.
Raise the temperature.
Increase the maximum output tokens.

questions.explanation: Examples are the most reliable way to communicate format, because they demonstrate rather than describe. A handful of well-chosen ones — including an edge case — usually beats several paragraphs of specification.

distractor_notes.C: Increases variance, which is the problem.

questions.stem: Which workload is the best candidate for a smaller, faster model tier?

options.text: Designing a migration strategy for a distributed system.
Extracting a date and an amount from 200,000 well-formatted invoices.
Debugging an intermittent race condition.
Reviewing a security-critical authentication change.

questions.explanation: High volume, low ambiguity, easily verified output — that is where a smaller tier delivers most of the quality at a fraction of the cost and latency. The other three are judgement-heavy and low-volume, exactly where capability earns its price.

analogy.text: It is right-sizing. Batch extraction is not the workload you provision for peak reasoning capacity.

questions.stem: For prompt caching to be effective, how should a prompt be ordered?

options.text: Variable content first, stable content last.
Stable content first, variable content last.
Alphabetically by section name.
Order is irrelevant to caching.

questions.explanation: The cache matches on a prefix, so anything that changes must come after everything that does not. Put the system prompt, tool definitions and large static documents first, and the user's question last.

distractor_notes.A: Invalidates the cache on every request.

analogy.text: It is layer ordering in a Dockerfile: copy the lockfile and install dependencies before copying the source, or every build busts the cache.

questions.stem: When does asking the model to reason step by step before answering genuinely help?

options.text: On every task, without exception.
On multi-step problems — analysis, maths, debugging, planning — where intermediate reasoning changes the final answer.
On simple lookups, to double-check them.
Only when the output must be JSON.

questions.explanation: Explicit reasoning helps where the answer depends on intermediate steps. On a simple retrieval it adds tokens and latency for nothing, and on a strict-format response it can actively interfere unless the reasoning is placed in a designated block.

distractor_notes.D: Reasoning and format are separate concerns — and unstructured reasoning breaks strict JSON.

questions.stem: An organisation's monthly agent spend has tripled. Select the THREE interventions most likely to reduce it without materially reducing value.

options.text: Enable prompt caching for stable prefixes such as system prompts and large reference documents.
Route bulk, low-judgement work to a smaller model tier.
Move latency-insensitive batch workloads to the Batches API.
Cap every engineer at ten sessions a day.
Turn off all automation.

questions.explanation: Caching, right-sized routing and batch pricing all reduce the cost of the same work. Hard usage caps and switching automation off reduce the work itself — that is not optimisation, it is cutting the thing you were buying.

distractor_notes.D: A blunt cap penalises the heaviest users, who are often delivering the most.
distractor_notes.E: Removes the value with the cost.

questions.stem: What does assigning a role — 'You are a senior database reliability engineer' — actually accomplish?

options.text: It grants the model access to specialised training data unavailable otherwise.
It sets expectations for vocabulary, depth and what the response should prioritise, which improves relevance on domain tasks.
It changes the underlying model that serves the request.
It has no measurable effect.

questions.explanation: A role is framing. It shifts which considerations get surfaced and at what depth — a DBA framing will raise locking and rollout risk unprompted. It unlocks nothing hidden and changes no infrastructure.

distractor_notes.D: The effect on relevance is real.

questions.stem: A response must be a JSON array and nothing else, but the model keeps adding a friendly preamble. Which technique addresses this most directly?

options.text: Prefill the start of the assistant's response with the opening bracket so continuation is constrained.
Add 'please' to the instruction.
Lower the maximum output tokens so the preamble is truncated.
Post-process with a regular expression and hope.

questions.explanation: Prefilling puts the model mid-structure, so there is nowhere for a preamble to go. It is the most reliable format control available, and it costs nothing.

distractor_notes.C: Truncates the payload, not the preamble.
distractor_notes.D: Fragile, and it is treating the symptom.

questions.stem: Two prompt variants are proposed for a production classifier. How should the choice be made?

options.text: Whichever reads better to the team.
Run both against a labelled evaluation set and compare accuracy, cost and latency.
Whichever is shorter.
Ask the model which prompt it prefers.

questions.explanation: Prompt changes have non-obvious effects, and human intuition about them is poor — a wordier prompt often wins, and sometimes the elegant one quietly loses three points of recall. Measure on real examples, on all three axes that matter.

distractor_notes.C: Brevity is not a quality metric.
distractor_notes.D: Not a source of ground truth.

analogy.text: It is A/B testing versus arguing in a design review. Prompts are code; hold them to the same evidentiary standard.

questions.stem: Which statement about extended thinking is correct?

options.text: It is free, since thinking tokens are not billed.
It has a configurable token budget, those tokens are billed, and it pays off on genuinely hard reasoning rather than on routine work.
It replaces the need for examples and clear instructions.
It guarantees a correct answer.

questions.explanation: Thinking is a budgeted, billed resource. Spend it where deliberation changes the outcome — planning, subtle debugging, trade-off analysis — and keep the prompt itself well specified regardless, because thinking does not compensate for an unclear question.

questions.stem: A prompt includes a 60-page document and a question about it. Where should the question go?

options.text: Before the document, so the model reads with purpose.
After the document, at the end of the prompt.
Split in half around the document.
It makes no difference.

questions.explanation: With long documents, placing the query after the content is the established guidance for Claude, and it happens to align with caching: the stable document forms a reusable prefix and the varying question sits at the tail.

distractor_notes.A: Loses the caching benefit and is not the recommended order.
distractor_notes.C: Fragmented instructions are harder to follow.
distractor_notes.D: Placement measurably affects both quality and cost.

questions.stem: An architect must forecast the cost of rolling an agent workflow out to 500 engineers. Which model is most sound?

options.text: Multiply one engineer's first-week spend by 500.
Model input and output tokens per task type, multiply by measured task frequency per engineer, apply cache-hit and batch discounts, and validate against a pilot cohort.
Assume cost scales with headcount only.
Use the vendor's list price for one seat.

questions.explanation: Spend is driven by tokens per task and tasks per person, not by headcount. Build the model bottom-up from measured task shapes, apply the discounts you will actually realise, then check it against a pilot before committing a number to a budget.

distractor_notes.A: First-week usage is unrepresentative in both directions — novelty inflates it, inexperience deflates it.
distractor_notes.C: Usage per engineer varies by an order of magnitude.

questions.stem: Which instruction is more likely to produce the intended behaviour?

options.text: 'Do not be verbose.'
'Answer in at most three sentences, then stop.'
'Avoid unnecessary words.'
'Never write too much.'

questions.explanation: Positive, specific and checkable beats negative and vague. 'At most three sentences' is a constraint that can be followed and verified; 'not verbose' requires the model to guess your threshold.

distractor_notes.C: 'Unnecessary' is doing all the work and is undefined.

questions.stem: A retrieval-backed assistant occasionally invents policy details not present in the retrieved documents. Which mitigation is most effective?

options.text: Instruct it to answer only from the provided documents, to quote the supporting passage, and to say explicitly when the documents do not contain the answer.
Lower the temperature to zero.
Use a larger model and assume the problem resolves.
Add 'do not hallucinate' to the prompt.

questions.explanation: Grounding works by making the source visible and giving the model a sanctioned way to decline. Requiring a quote makes unsupported claims obvious to a reviewer, and an explicit 'not found' path removes the pressure to fill the gap.

distractor_notes.C: Reduces frequency at best; the failure mode remains.
distractor_notes.D: The model has no reliable internal flag to consult.

analogy.text: It is the difference between an essay and a referenced report. Requiring the citation is what makes the unsupported claim visible.

questions.stem: Production prompts are edited directly in a dashboard by three teams. What is the main architectural problem?

options.text: Dashboards are slower than editors.
Prompts are production behaviour with no version control, review or rollback — a change with no diff and no author, deployed instantly.
Dashboards cannot store long prompts.
There is no problem if the team is small.

questions.explanation: A prompt is source code for behaviour. Without versioning you cannot review a change, attribute a regression, or roll back — the three things you rely on for every other production artefact.

distractor_notes.D: Small teams break production too, and they also lose the audit trail.

analogy.text: It is editing production configuration through a console with no change management. It works until the day it does not, and then you have no diff to look at.

questions.stem: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe prompt caching economics.

options.text: Writing to the cache costs more than an ordinary input token; reading from it costs substantially less.
Caching only pays off when the cached prefix is large and reused several times before it expires.
Cached tokens are free to write and free to read.
Caching increases output token cost.
A cache entry persists indefinitely once written.

questions.explanation: There is a write premium and a large read discount, so the break-even depends on reuse before expiry. A small prefix used twice may not repay the write; a large one used repeatedly in a session repays it immediately.
